extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets, writers, and literary readers seeking guidance on poetic/prose decorum and narration
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for composing serious poetry and prose and for credible narration: principles for truthfulness, appropriate use of classical mythology, poetic decorum, and rhetorical conduct (also includes advice on marital letters and publishing dreams).

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth as the foundation of beautiful thought
rubrics_metrics.description: “No Thought is beautiful which is not just, and no Thought can be just which is not founded in Truth, or at least in that which passes for such.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serious compositions should be grounded in truth (or plausible truth). Thoughts and images that are not just or founded in truth are not genuinely beautiful. Anti-pattern: decorating a subject with false or irrelevant fables that obscure the real action or character (e.g., inventing mythic machinery instead of describing real deeds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pagan mythology in serious Christian compositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not write in the Pagan creed for serious Christian poems — e.g., do not make Prince Eugene a favourite of Mars or carry on a correspondence between Bellona and a real marshal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strictly forbid presenting pagan gods as real agents in serious panegyrics or poems of national importance. Such recourse is called 'puerility' and shows lack of elevation. Permissible exceptions (see other entry): very short allusion or metaphorical use only; do not surrender the poem's Christian/realist credibility to classical machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict mythological references to metaphor, simile, or brief allusion
rubrics_metrics.description: If pagan deities appear at all, it should be 'in Metaphor, Simile, or any very short Allusion,' and with 'great Caution and Circumspection.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow brief classical allusion for poetic color, but avoid introducing gods as active characters. Anti-pattern: extended involvements of pagan agents or making destinies the causal explanation for real events except when justified by rhyme or parody.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow classical machinery in mock-heroic and certain comic uses
rubrics_metrics.description: In Mock-Heroick Poems, the Use of the Heathen Mythology is not only excusable but graceful, because the design is to adapt fabulous machines to low subjects and to ridicule such machinery in modern writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mock-heroic and parodic works may freely exploit pagan mythology to comic effect. Use of such machinery is appropriate when the intention is to satirize or invert the grandeur of the originals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use local/natural superstition in pastorals rather than antiquated fables
rubrics_metrics.description: Pastorals can be refreshed by substituting 'the superstitious Mythology which prevails among the Shepherds of our own Country' instead of the common ancient fawns, satyrs, and nymphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To make pastoral poetry more natural and original, draw on indigenous rural beliefs and figures rather than stock classical creatures. Example cited: Philips gave a new life to pastorals this way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus panegyric on real actions and character, not mythological episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: When celebrating a great man, the poem should not 'turn more upon Venus or Helen' or describe exploits of River-Gods; it must 'carry in it all the Colours of Truth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise should illuminate the subject's real deeds and virtues. Avoid substituting classical episodes or mythic episodes for concrete biography and achievement; readers who praise based on mythic allusion reveal they haven't perceived the subject's genuine merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer realistic causes and explanations in narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attribute real events (e.g., deaths in war) to the Destinies or pagan agency when a Christian/real explanation (e.g., 'Powder and Ball') suffices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve supernatural or mythic causation for metaphorical or poetic purposes only; avoid undermining credibility of a serious account by relying on fate or gods to explain ordinary phenomena. Exception may be allowed for rhyme or deliberate figurative usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid invoking the Muses or Phoebus in serious contemporary poems
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectation that the poet should 'make his own Poem, without depending upon Phoebus for any part of it, or calling out for Aid upon any one of the Muses by Name.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not resort to classical invocations as a substitute for original poetic invention. Such appeals are seen as a sign of dependence and puerility in modern (Christian) panegyric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider paralinguistic cues; tone and gesture carry force in narration
rubrics_metrics.description: In relations, 'the Force of the Expression lies very often more in the Look, the Tone of Voice, or the Gesture, than the Words themselves,' and repeaters often misinterpret when they cannot reproduce those cues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing or staging reported speech or narrative, attend to how nonverbal signals shape meaning; be aware that literal repetition by others often alters the original intention. Anti-pattern: assuming word-for-word repetition will preserve original meaning without noting tone/gesture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of narrative escalation and embellishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrations uttered with vehemence and authority often acquire additions — first the marvelous, then the impossible — and hence become unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for the tendency of storytellers to escalate events; a useful skeptical technique is to contest the single fixed way the narrator presents an event and point to other possible ways it could have happened. Example tactic described: disputing the settled single manner and leaving room for 'ninety-nine other ways.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize two kinds of liars/narrators: embellishers and reciters
rubrics_metrics.description: Two sorts of liars in coffee-houses: (1) those with 'much Impudence and a strong Memory' who literally repeat what they hear (reciters), and (2) those with understanding and smooth language who 'embellish' and are eloquent on certain heads (embellishers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate whether a report is mere literal repetition or an embellished account. Embellishers invent detail and rhetorical flourish; reciters mechanically transmit information — both are unreliable in different ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain the appearance of attention as a social rhetorical performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Good breeding obliges a man to maintain the figure of keen attention in a coffee-house; the 'true Posture' involves leaning over a table with the edge pressing the stomach — the more pain, the more gracious the bending over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prescriptive social behavior instruction functions as rhetorical performance: appearing to listen well flatters narrators and encourages them to continue. (Included as guidance on social presentation when receiving narrative material.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate poetic thought for justice and plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: No thought is beautiful which is not just; a manly panegyrick should 'carry in it all the Colours of Truth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing poetic or rhetorical passages, prefer those whose conceits are just and plausible rather than ornamented by inappropriate classical fables. (Closely related to 'Truth as foundation' but emphasized here for evaluative reading of poetry.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish only original or sufficiently strong dreams/visions
rubrics_metrics.description: When compiling Dreams and Visions, the editor resolved to 'Print nothing of that nature, which was not of my own Invention' and to suppress weak submissions: Epictetus's advice is quoted: 'Never tell thy Dreams... though thou thy self may'st take a Pleasure in telling thy Dream, another will take no Pleasure in hearing it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid publishing commonplace, weak, or derivative dreams. Allowances may be made for dream content given the dreamer's age, condition, or social standing, but generally prefer original, substantial visions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize dream/vision material by dreamer's age and condition
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting dreams, take into account the 'Age, Condition and Sex of the Dreamer' and make allowances accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers and editors should interpret visions with sensitivity to the dreamer's background; youthful or high-born dreamers may be judged differently from others. This is guidance for evaluating dream-genre submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary qualities recommended for choosing a spouse
rubrics_metrics.description: For choosing in marriage: 'A virtuous Disposition, a good Understanding, an agreeable Person, and an easy Fortune, are the things which should be chiefly regarded.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When weighing potential spouses, consider these four core attributes. If one must trade among them, prefer combined good faculties (e.g., understanding + moderate estate) over mere wealth. Anti-pattern: marrying solely for fortune or being swayed by fashionable wit lacking good-nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer talent plus moderate estate over mere wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: He that has 'excellent Talents, with a moderate Estate, and an agreeable Person, is preferable to him who is only rich,' because good faculties may purchase riches, but riches cannot purchase worthy endowments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When advising readers on marriage choices, place greater long-term value on character and ability than on wealth alone. Example: a man of sense who can better the wife's life is preferable to an unreflective wealthy husband.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value wit only when founded on good-nature and humanity; avoid restless, pleasure-seeking wits
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit and the capacity to entertain are valuable only if 'founded upon Good-nature and Humanity.' There are 'ingenious Men' whose abilities only make themselves and those about them uneasy — especially those 'far gone in the Pleasures of the Town' who cannot support life without constant excitement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discern whether a witty character is steady and humane or merely restless and insatiable; prefer the former for stable relationships and thoughtful prose characterisation. Anti-pattern: romanticizing the fashionable wit who becomes quickly sated and seeks new beauties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugal love is a higher, stabilizing refinement than amorous passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjugal Love 'is like the Vital Heat' — a more steady, refining force — whereas passion for a mistress 'resembles too much the Flame of a Fever.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In portraying or advocating love, prioritize the virtues of friendship, tenderness, constancy, and simplicity that sustain marriage over the transient excitement of flirtatious gallantry. For letter-writing and intimate prose, favour sincere, simple expression rather than extravagant encomium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor simple, sincere expression in letters to a spouse
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters by 'Men of Goodnature to their Wives' would, even with less elaborate style, have the advantage over the extravagant, flattering letters men write to mistresses; 'Friendship, Tenderness and Constancy, drest in a Simplicity of Expression, recommend themselves by a more native Elegance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing epistolary or intimate prose, prefer straightforward sincerity that conveys steady affection and moral worth rather than ornate, hyperbolic flattery.
